comments.author: Thai Thuong Triet
comments.text:
IS THERE AN ABSOLUTE TIME FOR THE ENTIRE UNIVERSE?
The concept of motion is always associated with matter, more specifically, motion is the change in position in space of the elements of matter. Images are not matter, so the concept of motion cannot be applied to images. In reality, we can only apply the concept of transmission to light, which is the movement that transmits energy through the method of transmission. Therefore, whether we want to or not, we must come to the conclusion that "the speed of objects cannot be compared to the speed of light." This conclusion has invalidated the conclusions of the theory of relativity, as there is a discrepancy in comparing the speeds of objects to the speed of light in the theory of relativity. However, we are discussing issues in the field of light, where reality and illusion always coexist, and mathematical models cannot be applied from the material world to the non-material world. Is this a form of motion, where light is just one case of this form of motion?

Returning to our main task of unifying the units of time for systems with any motion, if we can achieve this, we can assert that the results of the narrow theory of relativity are illusory presence. This task may seem difficult and unconvincing, but it turns out to be quite simple. Let's broadcast our running clock directly throughout the universe, to the spacecraft moving at different speeds in space. They will receive the same television program. The only difference is that those who are closer will receive the program earlier than those who are farther away. However, the speed, inertia, or non-inertia of the spacecraft cannot affect the television images that we have transmitted, just like the image of the sun always accompanies us, regardless of our movements. The movement of the clock is a sequential and continuous process over time, and it originates from the same source, so there will be no phenomenon of overlapping and chaotic images when they reach any camera. Therefore, although the current time on the spacecraft at different positions may not be the same as our source, the image and rhythm of the clock on the TV will be the official time on the spacecraft, meaning that all spacecraft share the same unit of time. In fact, this is just a simplified expression for easy understanding, because electromagnetic waves are completely different from light. The typical difference is the scale of electromagnetic waves, which is electrons, while the scale of light is photons. Furthermore, electromagnetic waves have a delay (delay caused by inertia or the magnetic field generated in electromagnetic oscillation), while light never has a delay like electromagnetic waves, so electromagnetic waves cannot replace light. This is the case on the scale of the universe, but within the narrow range of our small Earth, the task becomes even simpler. Place a fixed clock at a specific position, and the image of the clock on the moving mirrors relative to the fixed position of the clock will not change, regardless of the movement of the mirrors. Moreover, the clocks in the mirrors always move simultaneously with the actual clock (Objects and their images are always symmetric across the mirror plane. Therefore, any process from the object to the mirror and the image of the object in the mirror always occur simultaneously, or the image in the mirror is always simultaneous with the object being reflected.). With the current understanding of light and the inherent nature of the speed of light, we always have the illusion that we cannot observe the true state of all objects in the universe at a certain moment. Everything we see has already happened in the past and is overlapping and chaotic. Clearly, the results of the narrow theory of relativity are precise quantitative formulas for illusory phenomena, similar to performing calculations with negative numbers.
When we talk about speed, we refer to the movement of objects (matter) in space, but the speed of light is not like that. Imagine a series of stationary light bulbs being lit one by one, starting from the first bulb to the last at the speed of light. We will see that the series of bulbs is no different from a beam of light, which is how light operates. The constancy of the speed of light affirms that photons always remain stationary, acting as light bulbs to transmit light from the source to everywhere, and this is not contradictory to Galileo's principle. Since we cannot distinguish one photon from another, we must consider space as a continuous medium consisting of photons, transmitting interactions simultaneously between the forces and reactions. This means that once light reaches us from the source, from that moment onwards, we always instantaneously see the image of the source at that time.

Finally, let’s  answer the following question to know where the stage of our science is:
THEY ARE IN THE DISTANCE OF ONE BILLION LIGHT YEARS FROM US, SO WE OR THEM WHO IS BEING IN THE PAST OF ONE BILLION YEARS AGO?

The material world only exists in reality, while the past and future of the material world only exist in the intellectual cognition of human beings. Therefore, when studying the motion of the material world in reality, time is only mentioned in the concept of instantaneous velocity at the moment of observation.
The Theory of Relativity does not allow us to have concepts of absolute time and space, hence there is no concept of simultaneity and vector concept in multi-dimensional curved space. Current theoretical physics textbooks accept this theory yet still consider simultaneity as natural, deliberately ignoring the absurdity to the point of humor, and then applying Vector Analysis in mathematics to justify, turning theoretical physics into a mess as it is today.

Другите родени по-далече от Новата Година са с по-дълъг лъч светлина като характера им е по-арогантен и агресивен и техния лъч светлина е станал по-тънък и губи естественото си съпротивление против света на мъртвите - ада/времевата линия и черна материя която е навсякъде по всяко време и върху която се материализираме за да използваме материята да променяме следващата си рожденна дата и дължината с това на нашия личен лъч светлина който представлява нашата душа и личност.

Ние сме най-близо до Рая - света на Бог и най-далече от времевата линия и материята която трупаме върху нея/ада.
Всякеки отделен вид живо същество лъч на характер произлиза от отделна част на Бог, където Бог е извора на личните характери на всички живи същества върху които се трупа материя върху времевата линия и така душите са разделени също по видове. Но всички ние сме тук само временно за да изгорим всичко черно и лошо от чувствата си. В този живот сме чернилката на върха на пламъка на всяка свещ. In this view, space is not simply an empty medium, but rather the result of the superposition of two fundamental wave functions, called Eloi (\(E\)) and Meloi (\(M\)). These two waves with different wavelengths (\(L_{E}\) and \(L_{M}\)) quantize the geometry of space.

 Electromagnetic tensor (\(F_{\mu \nu }\)): The angular fluctuations and phase difference between the Eloi and Meloi waves give rise to the electromagnetic field intensity tensor. Gravitational tensor (\(R_{\mu \nu }\)): The stacking density resulting from the constructive interference of these two waves produces the curvature tensor, or gravitational field. In fact, mass is the rate of compression of the network of intersecting waves at a point.

Coupling coefficients: A mathematical coupling constant formulates the conversion of these wave frequencies into physical constants such as the electrical permittivity (\(\varepsilon _{0}\)) and the gravitational constant (\(G\)).

text:
[Join us at the Applied Interactive Multimedia Lab this semester/Summer]

Hi everyone! I’m a postdoc researching on Soft Haptics [https://aimlab-haptics.com/soft-haptics] with Prof. Mohamad Eid's Applied Interactive Multimedia Lab. I'm looking for a non-graduating summer undergrad research assistant who is interested in materials science, engineering, and robotics. You can choose from: Working with me and some soft robotics collaborators in-person in NYU NY if you are already in the US, working in the lab In NYUAD (pending regional developments), or completely remote. 35 hours per week, you can choose between 7~13 weeks (May 18-Aug 14). Wish to apply/re-apply? Please send me your up-to-date CV, transcript, and relevant materials to ken.iiyoshi@nyu.edu, titled "SRA26:Your preferred name" by April 5th. We'll send you an offer letter for the undergraduate research office funding application deadline by April 13th 5PM GST.

Your job would be to help us provide additional support in the following activities. We'll cater to your interests and make them fun!

-Soft actuator fabrication: mixing resins, spin coating them into films in a cleanroom, and assembling them into actuators.

-Actuator experimentation: Running experiments on arduino, recording thermography and videos, and making tables and plots from them.

-Make simulations for these using Genesis: [https://genesis-embodied-ai.github.io/]

The application is for a startup in robotics and the metaverse, including something like this attached gif!

Description of start and end dates: [https://students.nyuad.nyu.edu/.../summer-research-grants/]

comments.text:
I’m an econ minor so I can’t really speak on capstone but I did both my econ electives in nyc and they were soo interesting. 
I did a class called sports economics and it was my favorite class I ever took. I think it’ll only be really appealing if you’re into sports, but I also know a lot of people not into sports who took it. The content is very different to what you usually take and I feel like it presented very interesting povs on things. I would generally say it was easy-ish and the professor is an incredible lecturer he’s really passionate about this topic.
The second class I took was data bootcamp. This will likely help you with your capstone. It provides an introduction to data analysis and visualization with python. He starts from scratch so dw if you don’t have previous coding knowledge. The only annoying thing is that it’s on a stern curve and there is a participation grade even though I felt like there weren’t many opportunities to participate in the class unless you asked questions. But it was super chill overall. You have a midterm and final project, and then around 7 small homework assignments.

author: Beniamin Strzelecki
text:
It's this time of the year that many graduating students are considering master's programs in the US and as I'm wrapping up my MPA at Columbia University, I thought I could share a few reflections 

In some parts of the world, like Europe and China, master's degree is something you do right after your bachelor's degree because it's accessible, affordable and a social norm. I realised that in the US, this is really not the case for professional degrees – master's of public policy, business administration, education, environmental management and so on. These programs are targeted at people who need them to get promoted on their current job or those who want to pivot to a new field. While it's cool to meet mid-career professionals in your program (3-5 years of work experience), it also means that you will have to compete with them for summer internships and post-grad jobs. It's an uphill battle in an already tough job market that is unfriendly to international students (I made a post about it last year: https://www.facebook.com/groups/nyuad.room.of.requirement/posts/9587376384673563)

Just to be clear – this has nothing to do with the quality of education that you are receiving. I've learnt more than I expected and I love my program but I see from many of my classmates that your work experience pre-grad school is a huge determinant of where you can get after 

I'm a lot less familiar with degrees in humanities and arts, PhDs and other programs focused on further career in academia so others could speak about it. There are also career paths where you really need that graduate degree, like law and medicine. Lastly, if you got a good scholarship, it's probably still worth it to go for it because the chance might not repeat itself – which was the case for me. But if you're asked to sell a kidney to get next degree right after NYUAD, it's good to make sure that you have a clear plan of what you are going to do with it or are confident enough about breaking into the US job market to recoup the investment

author: Lovnish Julka
text: Any reviews about Advanced Game Theory with Shuo Liu? How's the workload/ exams/ grading etc.

comments.author: Aset Nukushev
comments.text:
Amazing course, if you are interested in game theory, take it 100%. The first half was nice, the concepts were pretty easy, just with much more rigorous proofs than in Intermediate Micro. The second half was a bit more challenging, but still manageable. Overall, I would say it was closer to math than econ, especially with formal notation and proofs, but there are a lot of applications in markets (mainly the same examples as in Micro though)

The Professor is great, he has slides which help a lot, but sometimes I got lost in his explanations, especially in the second half of the course. Reading the textbook helps a lot though, so keep in mind that. The problem sets were take home, 1 ps every 2 weeks, and some of the problems were taken from the textbook. Exams were definitely easier than the problem sets, we had 2 midterms and an oral final (was supposed to be written), and the midterms had 3-4 questions each. It was mainly theoretical questions + some computation to find an equilibrium or something, and knowing basic probability theory helps

The Professor is lenient with grading, he definitely wants everybody to get a good grade, but you do have to put in effort to show that you understand the concepts. We had 6-7 people left after add/drop, so I think he graded based on effort and understanding considering the oral final. Overall, it's not an easy class for sure, but would recommend 100%

comments.text: Recommend this course! Did three courses with Prof Boisen already (but not this one) and can say that her courses are inspiring and the class discussions engaging. Go to her office hours to talk about your essays and everything you're interested in — she’s a wonderful person. But I would not say the workload is light: in fact, she may be very demanding. She told me that, even in a time like this, during the war, she does not want to lower her expectations for students’ performance, since the university is already being accommodating on this, while some other professors are becoming more lenient with grades. That said, she is still a fair grader. But agree on the point that she has a bit heavy pre-class readings. Definitely reply or text me if you got any questions of her courses.

text:
**Midad Initiative Opens New and Accessible Pathway into Teaching in Abu Dhabi!**

As part of its revamped teacher talent approach, the Abu Dhabi Department of Education and Knowledge (ADEK) has launched Midad – a flexible, entry-level training program designed to equip passionate individuals with the skills needed to step into the classroom.

The initiative reinforces ADEK’s continued efforts to elevate the caliber and standards of education across Abu Dhabi’s private and charter schools by expanding and diversifying the educator pool.

Midad creates an accessible pathway into education, starting with a four-week bootcamp delivered through a flexible, self-paced model. Open to UAE nationals and long-term residents, the program enables individuals with diverse experiences and a deep understanding of UAE values to bring real-world perspectives into learning environments and help shape future generations. It is also valuable for parents who want to play a more active role in their child’s learning journey and support their development.

In this bootcamp, participants will be introduced to the core principles of effective teaching, including classroom management, teaching methodologies, understanding diverse student needs, integrating technology and AI into learning, and strengthening the UAE national identity and values.

Upon completion, participants can apply their skills in part-time teaching roles, while progressing through additional pathways and pursuing further teaching qualifications. High-performing participants will also be invited to apply to Kon Moallim Cohort 2 — ADEK’s flagship program offering a fully sponsored postgraduate diploma in education.

This step reflects ADEK’s commitment to strengthening the teaching workforce by welcoming individuals who combine knowledge, experience, and purpose. It ensures students in Abu Dhabi benefit from relevant and enriching learning experiences aligned with the emirate's continued drive for excellence in education.

comments.author: Nada Beltagui
comments.text:
Hi! I’m currently taking it with Mang. The syllabus is unified for all sections and you can find it on the IM website (https://intro.nyuadim.com). There, you can also see the schedule & even the lecture notes from both professors to get an idea of their style of teaching. 

The class is pretty chill honestly and it’s kind of what you make of it. Most assignments are quite simple, but it’s up to you to go above beyond or do the bare minimum and that can really change your experience. Mang LOVES to talk and discuss (and can sometimes get carried away). I wouldn’t say he’s the BEST professor, I definitely do still have plenty of doubts after every class but if you do put in the effort to personally ask him or go to his office hours, you’ll probably get your answers. I found it a bit difficult to follow along with him in the first bit of the course (where we covered p5.js) because sometimes he wouldn’t really explain the code in the most ideal way. Sometimes he would show code that has been written before, show us how it works and kind of roughly explain it. I personally find it more helpful if he actually wrote the code live and explained as it he wrote (which he did do sometimes, but not always). But the arduino section, despite being online, has been a bit more fun to follow along since he actually builds it with us. 

Pm me if you have any other questions!

comments.author: Sejona Sujit Das
comments.text:
welcome to my favourite city! i think the spaces you're looking for are mostly in old dhaka, which i'm not super familiar with.

but in dhaka city itself, you can visit the dhaka university area, which is one of the oldest and most historically preserved areas. go to TSC (imo one of best areas in dhaka to engage with student culture). check out curzon hall, the DU library, and modhur canteen (a cafe/student meeting space where many student political movements started and it remains completely preserved and has not been modernised). there's also bangla academy, shilpokola academy, drik, and nilkhet (literally an area with alleys crammed with ancient bookshops that are falling apart, but almost every book i read growing up was bought there). visit icsba for archives on unpartitioned bengal, baatighor which is a small but beautiful library, and chhayanaut, which is the biggest cultural hub for music and the arts in dhaka.

you also must go to new market, you will never see such a mix of people from different social strata and economic backgrounds shopping together elsewhere. try the small shingaras there, buy a saree from hawkers market, and visit noorjahan market and priyangon. i think one of the peak shared moments of womanhood in dhaka is frantically hunting for fabric at priyangon for your next salwar kameez and hundreds of women also doing the same alongside you. for souvenirs, you have to visit aarong.

dhakaiyas love to engage in cha and adda (tea and yapping). grab a tong er cha (roadside tea) whenever you can, especially at TSC. my favourite adda spots in dhaka are robindro shorobor (best motka malai cha in dhaka), the rooftop cafe at drik (i believe its called coffeegraphy), north end cafe, bengal boi (the shingara here with the green chutney is divine), jatra biroti. you should also take a morning walk at ramna park.

for food, the best is in old dhaka, but in the main city, try the chaap and jhalmuri at bailey road after sunset. the best fuchka and bhelpuri is at dhanmondi road no 2. have breakfast at star kabab atleast once, kacchi from sultan's dine, and you have to try BFC and ilish mach bhaji. also you're here during kalboishakhi jhor season, and i hope you see a jhor (storm) before you leave because dhaka is magnificent in the rain. if it looks like it will pour, you must arrange to eat khichuri.

author: Jad Shatnawi
text:
[POSTING FOR A FRIEND]

Hey everyone,

We're looking for writers and journalists to contribute to a print newspaper being launched as part of a marketing campaign for a UAE-based brand.

This is open to everyone , not just NYUAD students. All ages, all backgrounds, anyone over 18 who has something worth saying.

This is a real, physical newspaper. It gets printed, packaged, and hand-delivered to people across Dubai. 

What we're looking for:

Short, well-written pieces — 500 words maximum. We're open to most formats: opinion, personal essay, cultural critique, short narrative, photography, illustration. New pieces written specifically for this edition are preferred, but we're happy to consider pre-written work that fits the themes.

Some topics we'd love to see covered:

— The art of slowing down // morning rituals, doing one thing at a time, being present

— Dubai and UAE life // the expat experience, the city's quiet side, what home means to third culture kids

— Food, drink, and sensory experience // taste, ritual, the difference between consuming and actually enjoying, favorite coffee shops, top food finds

— Pop culture and celebrity // honest takes, sharp observations, things worth saying not just petty gossip

— Arab artists and creatives // music, film, visual art, critique or profile of someone worth knowing

— Local and regional commentary // culture, language, identity, what's changing and what isn't

— Something educational but young // a concept, theory, or idea explained in a way your group chat would actually understand

This list isn't exhaustive. If you have a piece you're proud of or an idea that doesn't fit neatly into any of the above, pitch it anyway.

What you get:

— Your work published in a printed newspaper distributed across Dubai

— Full credit and promotion of your name across the brand's social platforms

— New pieces written for this edition are paid (compensation is based on the material) 

— Pre-written submissions are unpaid but will receive the same credit and visibility

— This is a one-time edition for now, but the goal is to make it monthly...meaning anyone who contributes now has a real shot at becoming a regularly published writer

To submit or pitch an idea:

Email: myrnashatnawi@greencorp.ae //Subject line// Mantaro Monthly

WhatsApp: 0557194058

You can submit by end of tomorrow (23rd of April). Please note that what you send is what will be printed (if chosen) it will not go through further editing on our end, so make sure there are no spellling or gramatical errors. 

Looking forward to reading what you've got.

author: Tamer Al Awar
text: Hello guys, is it advisable to take fos 3-4 with linear algebra?

comments.author: Udaya Pandit
comments.text:
A lot of people told me not to do that, so generally not advised, but it’s not entirely uncommon with bioengineers. I did it and it was pretty stressful but turned out fine. You just need to be really consistent in working for each class even before exams. And get help from upperclassmen because resources will save u. Don’t try to be a hero and do it all without help. Every week, I had at least one and at most four quizzes on the same day. So you will really have to study most weekends. Plus hw and reports etc will never end.

The midterms weren’t at the same time (FoS was a week before LA) so they didn’t gang up until the final, where physics and LA were on the same day. Smth like that will probably happen again, so keep that in mind. 

It turned out fine because I did a lot of practice + got help from profs/recitation and upperclassmen/friends. It was pressuring tho and I never want to do that again ✊
  
Hope this helps!

comments.text: i did fos1-2 with linear algebra + FYWS, and fos3-4 with probstats + analysis1 + at least 8-hour lab work.... It is not 100% un-doable, but it is definitely a lot of work. author: Mateja Damchevski

Hello everyone,

My name is Mateja Damchevski, and I am a student researcher at NYU Abu Dhabi conducting an academic study that examines how a digital platform that connects residents with instructors for in-home swimming lessons can establish trust and demonstrate credibility.

This research is part of my undergraduate capstone project at NYU Abu Dhabi and is conducted under the supervision of Chinny Ogunro, Visiting Assistant Professor of Practice of Business, Organizations and Society at NYU Abu Dhabi. The study has received institutional approval.

I am inviting the following groups to participate:
• UAE residents who live in a community/building with an on-site swimming pool
• Swimming instructors working anywhere in the UAE

The survey takes around 15–20 minutes, and participation is voluntary. Your data will remain confidential and mostly anonymized, and will be used strictly for academic research.

If you are interested in taking part in a follow-up interview, you can indicate this at the end of the survey; a limited number of participants will be randomly invited.

author: Chelsea Wang
text:
**The Library Presents: Stress Less Fest**

Finals are here, so are we! Join us virtually all next week for some stress less activities, hosted by the NYUAD Library. 

**Pomodoro (Study with Me) **

Monday April 27 & Friday May 1, 5PM-7PM

Sprint to the finish during our Pomodoro sessions on Monday and Friday! The Pomodoro Technique is a time-management method designed to improve focus and productivity by breaking work into 25-minute intervals ("pomodoros") separated by 5-minute breaks. Developed by Francesco Cirillo, it promotes deep work, reduces burnout, and manages distractions. 

Drop in anytime and leave whenever you need.

**Library Office Hour Drop-In**

Daily, 12 Noon-1PM

Stuck on your research? Struggling with citations? Drop in and troubleshoot any final paper issues with a librarian. No appointment needed. 

**Creative Writing for Relaxation (Mindful Study Break)**

Tuesday, April 28, 5PM-6PM

Take a break from deadlines and exams and give your mind some room to breathe. This session is all about writing for the joy of it — no grades, no pressure, no experience needed. You'll be guided through a series of fun, low-key prompts designed to spark your imagination and help you unwind. 

**Virtual Vision Boarding**

Wednesday April 29, 5PM-6PM

This one-hour virtual workshop is your chance to step back, breathe, and reconnect with the bigger picture! We’ll be utilising guided reflective writing and a digital vision board to get a clear picture on what you’re working toward not only this semester, but beyond it. 

**Library Trivia Quiz (just for fun): **

Thursday April 30, 5PM-6PM

Join us for a fun trivia quiz all about libraries and literature! Open to all members of our NYU community, come along for some light-hearted fun.

text:
Hi everyone,

How’s CDAD-UH 1079 The Science of Making Music with Prof. Matteo Marciano and Prof. Andy Tillotson overall? Do you find the class worth taking and engaging, or do the quizzes (if there are any!) and the projects feel like trouble?

Would appreciate if you can share the syllabus also!

comments.text: I would love to connect! Prof. Matteo was amazing to take a class with but with the other prof, you can email me if you want more info on how physics taught by them is…

comments.author: Taib El Khatib
comments.text:
Hey, sorry for the late reply.
[Disclaimer: I'm from a scientific/engineering background & LOVE music- hence, this was my BEST core]

The class was very satisfying for someone curious about using both lenses to analyse music. From one side, with Prof. Andy (Completely different from his FoS version btw), we delved deep into the physics of sound, resonance, superposition..., and I admit that for someone with no prior physics/waves knowledge would have to put some effort to understand and solve the questions (It's not that type of core classes you just go into and start yapping/brainstorming).

On the other hand, the music production part with Prof. Mateo was less demanding and more hands-on and fun. Here, you'll enjoy the music more and put your physics knowledge to practise: from active listening to spectrum analysis, to basic mixing, all the way to synthesizing and composing. In this section of the class, you'll have to do less work outside class, unless you wanna jam and try things in the software yourself. 

Lastly, the distribution of both sections of the class is very close to 50%-50%, and I think all the efforts put in understanding the physics do reward you once your start playing with sounds and mixing.

DM me (te2189) if you have more questions or need the syllabus.

text:
# #NYUAnDHired 6: Summer Internship Grant Updates
## **STUDENT GOVERNMENT BITE — A SMALL UPDATE**

**from:** Aymane, Student Government President

**relevant team:** Executive Board

Last year, StuGov received complaints from students who were rejected from grants. Some students who were initially accepted later declined their awards, meaning that available funding could not always be redirected. We are happy to announce that, thanks to CDC's work on the issue,  their office intends to implement a waitlist system this year, so that if funding becomes available later, additional students may still have a chance to receive support. This will allow more students to receive the grant.

Student Government followed up with CDC regarding the Summer Internship Grant disbursement timeline for Cycle 1 awardees, after students raised concerns that funds may only be disbursed in mid-May despite the award email indicating an approximate two-week timeline.

CDC confirmed that, as of yesterday, Student Finance had not yet been instructed to clear the disbursement of Cycle 1 funds. That step has now been completed as of this morning. CDC explained that the disbursement had been paused while the university finalized decisions around summer programs and the support framework for internships this year. So now it's only a matter of Student Finance disbursing the amount to your account. 

Hope this helps!

author: Aisha Al Ketbi
text:
Social Care Scholarship - UAE Nationals
Hello Everyone,

I’d like to share an exciting opportunity for UAE national students and alumni who are interested in pursuing postgraduate studies in the social care / social sector.

The Department of Community Development (DCD), in collaboration with ADEK has launched a Social Care Scholarship aimed at addressing Abu Dhabi’s growing workforce needs in the social sector.

Eligibility Requirements:

- Must be a UAE National

- Requires an unconditional offer from an ADEK-approved university in an approved field.

- Minimum GPA of 3.0 on a 4.0 scale, or equivalent during undergraduate studies.

- Minimum score of 6.0 in IELTS Academic or 67 in TOEFL iBT

- National Service completion certificate (for male applicants)

- Successful completion of interviews and required assessment

Interested students can apply via the registration link: https://ads.adek.ae/en/masters-overview

DCD are also exploring the possibility of holding an informational workshop. If this sounds relevant to you or someone you know please feel free to share and reach out. I’d be happy to provide more information and answer any questions!

author: Dea Likaj
text:
Hi everyone! Sharing this on behalf of one of our NYUAD professors, who has been working on a free Eurovision rating app called 𝟏𝟐 𝐩𝐨𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐬. It is both a fun way to rate the songs and a research project on musical taste across cultures. If you are into Eurovision, music, or just want to try something interesting, check it out below!

"Not sure how many of you follow Eurovision, but I know there are many Europeans in our community who might be quite into it.

I am pleased to share 12 Points, something I have been quietly working on for a while with collaborators at the University of Southern Denmark.

12 Points is a free app for rating every Eurovision entry, this year and in future editions. You can browse the competing songs, record your reaction to each one, build a personal scorecard, share it with whoever needs to know your verdict, and see how your taste compares with others.

But it is also a research project. Every rating will be anonymized, aggregated, and collected responsibly, following GDPR and research ethics guidelines. It helps us study how musical taste varies across cultures and countries, and what individual preferences reveal when hundreds of thousands of them add up into a collective verdict. Does the winner actually reflect what most people love? Or does the way we make group decisions shape the outcome in ways we do not fully appreciate? Eurovision is a great place to explore these sorts of questions and more.

If you are into music and especially Eurovision, you will enjoy it. But if not, no worries. You do not need to be a Eurovision fan to find the idea interesting. You just need opinions about music, which I suspect most of you have.

Free, no ads, open to everyone everywhere. The contest kicks off on May 12 and the Grand Final is on May 16 in Basel. But you can join and start rating the songs right now.

- iOS: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/12-points-citizen-science/id6762058508

- Android: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=science.points12

- Web: https://12points.science

Would love to see where you all land on the scoreboard!"

Join Music Technology Fundamentals (MTF) this Fall 2026 (MUSIC-UH 1002)
Make Music & Learn the Technology Behind Today’s Creative Industries 

Fall 2026 | Mon 9:55–11:10 AM & Wed 9:55 AM–12:25 PM 

Are you curious about how songs are produced, how sound is recorded, how beats are built, or how music is mixed for film, games, and digital media? MTF is an all-in-one introduction to the creative world of sound & music production. 

No advanced experience required, just curiosity! 

In this course, you'll explore: 

Music production using Logic Pro, Pro Tools, Ableton Live, and Max 

Digital audio, MIDI sequencing, sampling, and synthesis 

Mixing, editing, arrangement, and song 

Binaural, Immersive audio, acoustics, psychoacoustics, and signal flow 

The role of music technology in careers across music, film, media, games, and sound design 

Whether you are a musician, filmmaker, producer, or someone who wants to understand how sound works, this course will give you the foundation to create, record, shape, & think critically about music and audio in the digital age.

author: Míra Schlotter
text:
Hello everyone,

Quick course advert for Fall: "South Asia in the Indian Ocean World" (HIST-UH 1125X) with Professor Kulshreshtha - it's a history course, but also fills the X requirement.

I took an art history course with the same professor, she was very understanding, gave constructive feedback and was always ready to help.

Here is the course description:

"The course offers an in‐depth study of the history and culture of the South Asians, who comprise the majority population of the United Arab Emirates. Situated at the center of the Indian Ocean world, the Indian subcontinent is currently home to over a billion people, and is the site of richly interconnected histories with regions around the wider Indian Ocean, including the Gulf. The course explores these histories, with a focus on understanding major cultural, political, economic, and social connections and changes as they affected ordinary people (including migrant laborers) and shaped the nature of collective identities (ethnic, national, religious, caste, class, gender, regional, and linguistic) over time. In developing an understanding of how collective identities were produced historically, students ultimately acquire valuable tools for appraising and navigating competing models of nationalism, cosmopolitanism, and universalism in the wider Indian Ocean world today."

author: Sami
text:
Urgent: Need help reaching out to Global Ed
Case 1:

My Emirates ID expired in August 2025 while I was on my '1st' LOA (for Fall 2025). And since, as a Bangladeshi, I would need a One-Time Entry Permit to enter the UAE again, I started mailing them periodically about it starting from mid October.

Three "we're looking into it"s later come January 12 2026, 6 days before my scheduled flight, I get an email from Ms. Aisha Ali and Katya Grim instead of the immigration dept. They called to reveal that the UAE has a Visa ban on BD for over 6-7 months, smth they couldn't/didn't realize until less than a week before my flight. At that point claiming to have nothing to do, they just, administratively, placed me on another LOA

During the said meeting they also promised 2 things:

1. If the visa situation isn't resolved by next semester and they can't bring me back to AD, they'll arrange to send me on another Study Away. I am (or was) a rising senior year btw.

2. During this time, to make good use of this consecutive semester long hiatus, the CDC and ARC will help me to their capacity should I need anything.

Case 2: About the 2nd promise:

The CDC after finalizing my internship grant last week, retroactively cancelled it citing that I needed to be an 'actively enrolled student' to be eligible and since I'm on leave, I'm out of luck.

I explained the context surrounding my circumstancial LOA and how it was beyond my control. The rough summary of their response was "we get it but yeah, no".

I dropped it as is.

Case 3:

It's the end of May now which is way beyond the usual timeline for study away preparations.

They still haven't said anything conclusive of what I should expect next semester. After my last email to Aisha Ali I bet my friend that it'll be at least 2 weeks before I get another "we're looking into it" response. 

It's been a month since that email. And their last word was over 2 weeks before that.

I'm open to any and all suggestions atp since I can't seem to get a hold of them myself, and I don't have any precedents to go off of, with very little time left. Can't risk leaving anything till the last moment after what happened last time around.

Tia

P.S: If anyone currently on campus can pay a visit to Aisha Ali's on my behalf, it'd be a great help.

author: Mehdi Marrakchi
text: To NYUAD graduates who are still living in Abu Dhabi, any advice on things to look out for while looking for places to rent in Reem/Masdar/Saadiyat, and what the typical price range would be, whether renting furnished over unfurnished makes sense financially or not, and whether the utlities ( electricity and water) are included in the price or if that's something I will be covering myself? Just overall any tips you have/ mistakes you made that would be helpful to know, thank youuu!!

comments.author: Aya El Mir
comments.text: Bump and feel free to pm!

comments.author: Safeya Alblooshi
comments.text:
I’ll always advise unfurnished as you can easily buy decent furniture from IKEA at a good price instead of paying 10k per year for rent. Unless you’re staying for a short term rent like 6 months then definitely get furnished. Utilities are usually not included unless the owner specifically mentions it (not common); some buildings that are owned by a sole owner and not landlords cover AC as part of the total rent but not water/electricity.  
I would say always ask for a discount on total price because why not. Take photos of any issues you see so you’re not responsibly for it later. Check for any leaks and mold inside bathroom and kitchen cabinets. If you can and if you know a building is owned by a single company or owner (meaning you don’t deal with private landlords but a developer or person who owns the whole building), try to go to the building reception you’re interested in directly or call the developers directly to ask if there are available units to avoid dealing with an agent and paying agency fees. 
Saadiyat (NYUAD side) rent average these days are 70-85k for studio and 90-110k for a 1bd. Other sides of Saadiyat are considerably higher. Reem is slightly less and Masdar too.

comments.author: Skylar Marie Welte
comments.text: feel free to message me for a breakdown! living in Khalifa City (10 mins from masdar)

comments.author: Yeva Stepanova
comments.text:
Make sure you have the landlord’s contact number because communicating though an agent is a headache. Check in the contract how much the landlord is responsible for reimbursing you in case of major maintenance expenses (e.g. they reimburse you if you’ve paid over X amount of money for fixing something in the apartment). 
Before you move in, you have a chance to point out any issues with the apartment and ask for those to be fixed: leak damage, mould in the AC ducts, drainage, water heater, leaky taps and bidet sprayers, wall paint. Another big thing is improper rain insulation but that would be hard to check until the rainy season hits😬 
Also - check the building that you want to rent on Google maps because tenants will sometimes leave a review pointing out major issues.

Alternatively, just coming on a tourist visa to Dubai to get the GV is also a good option (ppl have done this in the past, but I'm not sure if it's still the case). But in both cases, you'd have to leave the country afaik.

MALE PARTICIPANTS NEEDED FOR FMRI STUDY - UP TO 300 AED 

Here for the summer and curious about how your brain works? 

Join our exciting research study and help us uncover how your brain processes memory! 

The Sreenivasan Lab is recruiting participants for a psychology experiment regarding how certain activities may impact working memory. We're using cutting-edge MRI technology to explore brain activity, and we need participants like you!

Eligibility requirements: You are eligible to participate if you are a male between 18 to 40 years old, right-handed, have normal or corrected to normal vision, are not colorblind, and do not have a history of brain injury, brain surgery or neurological condition.

Experiment details: The experiment may consist of two sessions. Each session will last about 2.5 hours. During the study, participants will be asked to complete short activities designed to explore focus and perform a computer-based working memory task inside the fMRI. Some physiological data (saliva samples) will be collected throughout the experiment. All measures used to collect this data will be non-invasive. 

You can receive Amazon vouchers worth 30 AED per 30 minutes or research participation credits. 

Interested? Check this form to see if you're eligible: 

https://forms.gle/HGrGEpVHConH7kQw5 

If you are eligible to participate, I will reach out to you to schedule a slot!

If you have any questions, concerns or want to know more about the experiment, you can email ja4261@nyu.edu

author: Sashini Manikandan
text: Guys, incoming freshman this side, a very random question as I went through the Albert Portal, why are majority of the classes only on Monday and Wednesday and can any upperclassmen (majoring in CS/Engineering) give me tips or advice on how to plan the classes to avoid burnout on these days ?

comments.author: Hiyath Peiris
comments.text:
It’s very normal to have that pattern. Monday-Wednesday and Tuesday-Thursday for lectures and Fridays for recitations/labs

If you are undecided on CS or Engineering, pick Computer programing for engineers as it counts for both majors (you need to get an A- and above for it to could towards the CS degree requirements) 

Try to take a FWYS class and calculus. These usually have a lot of sections so there’s ample room to pick a class that doesn’t fall back to back with your other classes. 

For the remaining 4 credits, you could do a Core class or another CS/Eng requirement depending on how you want your schedule to be. 

Another idea is it’s fine to have a two classes falling back to back especially if it’s a lecture and recitation. We all have gone through that hassle at least once in our lives and it isn’t that bad. You should just be more prepared on those days like eat well, hydrate yourself well so you aren’t starving or fall asleep.

comments.author: Shrisha Koirala
comments.text:
Freshman fall, I had 5 classes on M/W, and it was horrible (I was taking PE too, that's why 5). Please DO NOT take all classes on the same day. No matter how much you tell yourself that you can do it, it'll be horrible.

3 classes on Mo/We, and the other one on Tu/Thu is fine.

Now, regarding how to plan your classes. I started as an engineering major, and in the second semester, I changed to CS. If you're undecided, I recommend taking CPE (A/A- in CPE counts for Intro to CS), Calc (or MVC, whatever you place into), FYWS, and a core in the first semester. However, if, before course registration, you choose CS, you can replace the core with Discrete Mathematics. It's a pre-req for other courses, so the faster you get done with it, the better. 

And to avoid burnout, try to plan classes so that you have some break in between classes, especially for meals. I had a horrible meal schedule the first semester since I had 3 classes continuously from 9:55 to 2:00, so my first meal of the day was at 2:30 PM. Avoid that at any cost. 

Keep in track with your classes from the very beginning, and you'll be fine!

comments.author: Shrisha Koirala
comments.text:
Hi, I started uni with the Mech Engineering track. I recommend you take CPE, Calc (or MVC if you clear the assessment), FYWS, and Core in the very first semester. It is important to take CPE early since it's a pre-req for Design and Innovation. Completing Calc/MVC early will also set you comfortably in your four-year plan.

I don't recommend taking a colloquium in the very first semester. It is very writing-heavy and extensive, so it's preferable to get done with your FYWS and practice university-level academic writing before taking a colloquium. 

The first semester is the best time to explore a core that you might be interested in, but hesitate to take because you've never really been exposed to that subject area. 

Enjoy!

FoS 1-2 and CPE are interchangeable so you’ll do one 1st sem and the other 2nd sem, though I’d recommend taking CPE first bcs it’s a simpler introductory course + as Shrisha said it’s a prereq for D&I and ideally you should do that in January

author: Shinyi Kang
text:
# Participants Wanted! Interview Study on Everyday Digital Life

Hello! I'm Shinyi, Class of 22/23 alum, now based in Zurich, Switzerland 🙂

We are looking for participants for an interview study on how people use digital technologies in their everyday lives. **All adult digital users are welcome**!

* Who can participate?: **Adults aged 18 or older** who use a smartphone, tablet, or computer at least four days per week. Must be able to participate in the interview in English.
* What does participation involve?: A one-on-one interview lasting between 30 and 75 minutes, conducted via video call or in-person. The interview will ask about your everyday digital routines and how you use digital tools and platforms. The interview will be audio-recorded.
* Compensation: Participants will receive compensation equivalent to** 50 US Dollars **(approximately 40 CHF / 184 AED) in the form of vouchers or direct payment upon completion.

Interested? Please complete a brief pre-screening survey here (https://forms.cloud.microsoft/e/4UHYtHbA3B).

For questions, contact me at shinyi.kang@uzh.ch.

This study is conducted at the University of Zurich, Institute for Communication and Media Research (IKMZ), under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Tobias Dienlin.

comments.text: Hospital's as a whole institute they dont really usually recognize the insurance (happened to me too) but if you see the direct pay providers - by individuals doctors, usually it's fine! However, email/try calling them before the appointment to make sure they take it. That's how I was able to get it to work it. comments.author: Nasiba Akhmadullaeva
comments.text: Francisca Gonzalez Romero what does direct pay mean? i’m so confused🥹 like i can go and not pay, it will be covered by my insurance?

comments.author: Francisca Gonzalez Romero
comments.text: YES!!! it's like they are already agreeing to do so- and you can get an appointment in the same portal. On geoblue online it allows you to find doctors that allow that direct pay, however, make sure to call first

comments.author: Ayberk Cmn
comments.text: Download the bcbs (blue cross blue shield) and log into your student health plan. In the app click providers and select hospitals. You will be able to see hospitals that agreed to work with bcbs. Then, go to direct pay and request a direct pay (book an appointment from the hospital before). It takes around 24-48 hrs for the direct pay guarantee of payment to be sent to the hospital. Call the hospital’s insurance and/or international patient desk before your visit to confirm your direct pay. You usually don’t have to pay anything at the hospital, If they request a payment email or call bcbs directly.

comments.text: Yana Peeva Doesn't general engineering now have chemical engineering as one of the tracks?

comments.author: Yana Peeva
comments.text:
Aleksandar Boljević Yes! Now it does. To do that within the 36 credits of 
 Engineering electives, 
you take the foundational Chemistry classes at NYUAD and then Chemical Engineering specialized courses at NYU Tandon. You can also take directed studies with engineering professors (but probably not with chemistry faculty). You can specialize even further if you’d like and focus on Chemical Engineering for the oil/petroleum industry, for cosmetics, for environmental studies, etc. Prof. Margaret Julias, who is our Dean of General Engineering, is a Chemical Engineer by education so she is an excellent resource in planning a 4year plan for Chemical Engineering at NYUAD. Also, internships in summer are super important: make sure they are all Chemical engineering R&D or at least supporting roles in chemical departments at big companies. Feel free to PM if you have other questions.

author: Sameer Kamran
text:
German Grad School

author: Areebah Farooq
text:
Hello,
I'm a rising sophomore in CS and could use some advice on planning out my sophomore year.
Last spring I took Data Structures and Discrete, and taking them together with a FYWS was challenging. Then, I did Multivariable Calc over the summer which was also rough lol. So, this year I really want a balanced schedule instead of dumping all the hard courses into one semester.
I'm thinking of spreading LA, CSO, CN, and Algo across the year, since CSO and Algo are prereqs for the second study away and I want them done in time. My plan is to keep fall lighter, just one of these four plus some gen electives and core requirements, and then take the rest of the challenging courses in spring, since I'm planning to study away in Paris that semester.
Does that sound like a reasonable way to balance things out? And if you've taken these, which one would you start with in the fall?

LA and Algo will both be hard, but the professors you choose can rlly affect your experience, just try to stay on top of assignments for both courses and inshallah it won’t be horrible !!

But I would really recommend doing algo and LA in abu dhabi with some cores or gen electives, then doing CSO and CN in Paris along with French (and if you haven’t done your CDAD yet I would recommend taking principles of data science in paris. author: Mohamed Bahgat Hussein
text:
current engineers or engineering students please help
I am an incoming student who’s planning on doing engineering. During my senior year, I initially wanted to do chemical engineering (I was particularly interested in the renewable energy industry.) I applied to NYUAD thinking that I would be able to specialize in chemical engineering while studying general engineering, but I later realized that I don’t actually get a ChemE degree. 

Right now, I am not sure which branch of engineering I should do, and honestly I am not sure if I want to study engineering at all. I am good at Math and very interested in studying the STEM subjects (especially chemistry), but I just don’t know why I want to do engineering it just seems like the “logical” thing to do because Im only interested in STEM.

I would really appreciate it if you clarify the ChemE track at NYUAD and give your opinion on my situation.

 please let me know if you’re interested in doing a zoom session with me to discuss this further.

comments.author: Akram Ehab Khairi
comments.text: I'm not familiar with the ChemE track at NYUAD but as an engineering alumni, my general piece of advice is not to go into engineering (or any major for that matter) just because it seems like the "logical" thing to do. I would recommend taking the time exploring what potential careers you could get into from your degree and speaking to people in those careers (bonus if they graduated from NYUAD) to see how you would fit into that. I enjoyed 10% of the courses I did during my MechE degree but it was for the sake of getting into a career I enjoy. Also with NYUAD, you can always change your mind and pivot but it's good you have some form of initial idea with the STEM subject area.

comments.author: Mujtaba Kamran
comments.text: From what I understand you can major in Chemistry through the Sciences division and use some general electives for engineering related courses or do a double major or major/minor track.

author: SH Al
text:
One of my professors asked me to help spread the word about this course, and I honestly couldn’t recommend it enough.

Women and Work in the Gulf is being offered this fall by Professor Sara Musaifer. It’s a fascinating course that explores women’s experiences, labor, gender, and social change across the Gulf region. I’ve had the chance to learn from this professor before, and she is truly one of the most engaging and thoughtful instructors I’ve had. She creates a welcoming classroom environment, encourages meaningful discussions, and makes every topic feel relevant and interesting.

If you’re looking for a course that will challenge you to think critically while learning about important issues in our region, I highly recommend checking it out!

author: Sadijon Akilov
text:
Hello, guys! I’m an incoming freshman for Fall 2026. I’ve chosen the following courses: Intro to CS with Kassab, Calculus with Applications to Science and Engineering with Fayad, and Discrete Math with Mahmoud.

For my fourth course, I couldn’t get into any of the FYWS classes, so I chose Communication and Technology with Uma Hussain. What do you guys think about this course?

comments.author: Nada Beltagui
comments.text:
Hi! I think this is a really tough course load for your first semester. I don’t know about the difficulty of communications and technology as I haven’t taken it, but calculus, intro to CS, and discrete all have weekly assignments/hws, quizzes, midterms, and finals. 

They are not necessarily difficult courses but considering this is just your first semester and you’re adapting to a new environment, it might to much work and deadlines of different classes are very likely to overlap. I would suggesting dropping one of the classes and taking a core instead, either an “easy” one or something you’re interested in. 

If communications and technology isn’t too difficult, it could be a reasonable fourth course.

comments.author: Ziya Vhora
comments.text: Comms and tech with Ume Hussain… I took this class. I’m presuming you’re planning to double major with IM, as Comms and tech isn’t required for minors (from what I remember, if the reqs didn’t change) - I’d say hold off on comms and tech until later semesters when the rest of ur classes aren’t as tough and demanding. Bcos Calc + intro to cs + DM is already tough and the timelines for midterms, finals, quizzes and such are very close by. I’m not sure which one is your capstone major, but I’m assuming it’s CS because you’re mostly taking CS classes. If that’s the case, I’d say prioritise taking CS + DM + CALC and do any core/colloqium that’s available. Comms and Tech is actually very demanding and it took up a lot of my time - I had to do part of the class online as well so I was able to receive some reprieve, but doing a full semester of comms and tech in person coupled with those three classes seems like a tough position.

comments.author: Ziya Vhora
comments.text: Comms and Tech will require you to do a final project as well - so you’d have to balance that with the Intro to CS project as well (I also took this class). The prof for Comms and Tech requires you to be fully engaging with the readings and demands a lot from reading responses. I’m not saying this to frighten you at all - at the end of the day it’s up to you -  but I’d recommend dropping comms and tech for now and taking another course. If you need more info you can pm me!

author: Parth Sanjay Badgujar
text:
HI Guys 

**Looking for experiences in CPE hows the course like and what advice would you guys  give to score A or higher **

comments.author: Shrisha Koirala
comments.text:
Be consistent. That's the best advice I can give.

Attend all the lectures, keep up with the course load, and don't leave any assignment for last.

Also, you'll have a team project. DO NOT PROCRASTINATE. Meet up every week from the very beginning and put in consistent work so that it doesn't pile up at the end and kill you.

Quizzes are easy, so try to score full on all of them. The final exam was hard, but you don't have to worry much about it if you do well in everything else.

Assignments are, well, umm, they're okay, but as soon as you get the assignment, start working on it. And utilize the office hours.

comments.author: Parth Sanjay Badgujar
comments.text: Shrisha Koirala thank you so much for such insights

comments.author: Bani Pala
comments.text:
Shrisha Koirala I second this!! Parth Sanjay Badgujar 
Try to get maximum grades on quizes and the assignments especially since they carry a lot of grade. We didn't have mid terms but had finals, which was a bit challenging, but if you've put efforts all semester, it shouldn't bring your final grade down. For the team project as well, keep working on it weekly so that you don't have to struggle at the end and definitely keep in touch with your project mentor and get insights from them. As someone who didn't know coding at all, I was able to pass the class with good enough grades so you should be fine as long as you make efforts.

comments.author: Anita Naseer
comments.text:
Since Shrisha gave a general breakdown I’ll focus on assignments and team project: for the team project make sure you’re all sharing your work evenly (if one person does all of it, it might be flagged during your presentation and cause grade deductions) and that you’re generally aware of what each other is doing. I’d advise you to choose as simple a project as possible and execute it well using the material you’ve learnt in class rather than trying something insanely complicated. The mentors you will be assigned will be useless by design (as in previous years there were cases of them doing a lot of the team’s work) so I would recommend reaching out to lab instructors, TAs, the prof, Reddit, really anywhere you can in case you’re stuck (even ROR!) 

The assignments are pretty tricky. In the fall sem they made it so AI wouldn’t work on the assignments (like our 2nd one was on trajectories which was notoriously hard for models at the time). Do NOT try to leave it to 1-2 days before the deadline, they take a lot of brainstorming and research, sometimes asking your friends. I’d really really recommend sitting down with the TAs if you’re really struggling to crack an aspect of the assignment or you have 0 idea where to begin, that’s what I did (shoutout to my lovely TAs) and it helped me out a lot in coming up with a plan. Our first two assignments were basic C++, third one was OOP focused and last one was MATLAB. 

The assignments typically consist of a report that holds way more marks for showing your research, your logic (algorithm), input/output diagrams, test cases. Make sure you give all of these a lot of time and attention as they constitute a big chunk of the grade. My code was faulty in some cases and I still got an okay grade because my reports made sense. 

As for research, which you will absolutely need bcs some of the things asked won’t be in syllabus and will require creativity and you looking for answers (especially for team project!) the professors want you to show where you got your info from, so credit everything you use and try not to get all your information from AI. And if you do use AI, make sure you credit its use because the prof might question you if they see your assignment code uses knowledge you weren’t taught in class or the textbook.  Especially if you run your code through AI to debug it, the AI might add new things to troubleshoot/streamline your code so make sure you go through the new code and understand every new feature THOROUGHLY bcs you might get questioned. 

The fall sem was def a lot stricter than spring sem but in general it’s not a hard class the workload is just heavy and the profs want you to really understand the logic behind the code.

comments.text:

2. There’s plenty of walking so ensure to bring comfortable shoes - ppl in NY mostly walk.
3. If you’re taking classes in other buildings like in Brooklyn or in Manhattan there are NYU Shuttles to take you there so you don’t need to worry about commuting as much. 
4. I’d suggest transferring at least some money into another bank account before you leave for NY in case your FAB card gets blocked abroad - and FAB is rlly annoying to contact for such matters, and it’s happened to me in NY before. 
5. You’re able to open a Student Checkings account at Chase Bank so that’s quite handy. 
6. It goes get chilly and then very cold later in the semester, so I’d recommend buying a good number of winter clothes.

comments.author: Shrisha Koirala
comments.text:
This is a very manageable first sem schedule. Fayad is an amazing professor, so just attend the lectures and recitations and do your assignments on time, and you'll be okay. His slides are very comprehensive and will help prepare you for the quizzes as well as the exams. He's also very helpful. Make use of his office hours. 

I didn't personally take Intro to cs, but my friends took it with Potsch, and you got yourself a great professor there. Apparently, he's amazing at explaining, and his exams as well as assignments are also fair. As far as I remember, you get pop quizzes every 2 weeks. But make sure to be very careful with all the assignments and quizzes since 1 mark equates to 1 percentage of the final grade.

FYWS should be alright. Just maintain your consistency throughout the semester, and you don't have to worry much. Utilize your professor's office hours a lot. Your writing instructor will also help you a lot. 

The one I'd recommend you pay extra attention to is discrete mathematics. It's not undoably hard, but it requires a lot of practice, especially with Professor Mahmoud. Her exams are harder than with other professors, so you'd do best by staying up to date from the very beginning and going out of your way to practice questions.

This is all. Aayush had almost the same schedule his first semester, except that he took core instead of FYWS. He did well and had a balanced schedule, so it should be fine.

comments.author: Anita Naseer
comments.text:
the workload for CPE can be challenging if you’re not keeping up with assignments as soon as they’re released. There is a strict AI policy and a focus on you doing your research and showing your sources if you include out-of-syllabus code. (Unless the syllabus has changed, I took it with Mohammad Eid), it’s 3-4 assignments. The first ones are basic C++, there’s one focused on OOP, and one on MATLAB. I have heard that it is much heavier than Intro to CS’s workload. 

My biggest recommendation for the team project you will get is to work together on as much as possible since during your presentation you will be questioned on what everyone did. I’d also recommend choosing the simplest project possible even if it sounds silly, the goal is to do something simple well rather than do something overly complicated and have it filled with bugs. 

The exams can be challenging but really lock in on the cheatsheet (these were allowed in fall sem, not in spring sem, so not sure if you’ll have these) but typically the exam doesn’t have a heavy weightage bcs it’s difficult.

text: Hi can someone suggest good Driving schools in Abu Dhabi? I need a license fast and also affordable 😅

comments.author: Saher Khaled
comments.text:
So to get a driving license in abu dhabi

You need first to do an eye exam/test then open a traffic file through tamm

Then you need to go to EDC (emirates driving company) and register for theoretical classes (online classes)
Then register for a theory exam at EDC
 
Once you pass(36/45 is the passing grade if I remember correctly)
Then you can sign up for driving school classes inside the EDC 
(The cheapest option is 16 classes in 16 days and you can take it in less time but more expensive)

After you finish EDC classes (in person) you do a parking test inside the school (parallel parking and 90-degree parking)

After you pass the test you apply for a training license through Tamm 

Then youcan sign up for driving classes with an external instructor (driving in Abu Dhabi) you need minimum 6 hours

After that the instructor will issue you a training certificate then you can apply for the police driving test 

Once you do it and pass the test you can apply for your driving license in Tamm

Keep in mind that this process will take around a month and will cost around 4000-5000 AED

author: Allen Kurban
text:
Philosophy and Physics at the Intersection
Hi RoR!

Professor Kevin Coffey will be teaching “PHIL-UH 2910: Philosophical Puzzles at the Atomic Scale: Measurement, Chance, and Spooky Action at a Distance” (Previously titled: Philosophy of Quantum Mechanics) next semester. If you’re interested not only in quantum mechanics but also in the different ways of interpreting what quantum mechanics tells us about reality, I’d highly recommend taking a look at this course. It’s a rare opportunity to explore questions at the intersection of physics and philosophy — questions about measurement, probability, reality, and the nature of the physical world.

The course also counts toward the Math major, so it’s a great way to satisfy a requirement while trying something outside the usual mathematics curriculum

I am copying the course description by the professor below:

‘The legendary physicist Richard Feynman wrote in his Lectures on Physics that “[a]lthough it is interesting and worth while to study the physical laws simply because they help us to understand and to use nature, one ought to stop every once in a while and think, ‘What do they really mean?’”. This course is an attempt to do just that for the physical laws governing the quantum domain. We know that the world they describe is profoundly weird, but it turns out that there are radically different and incompatible ways of making sense of that weirdness—ways that are grounded as much in philosophical and conceptual considerations as they are in experimental data. For example, what does it mean for a particle to be in a superposition? We know how to represent such a state mathematically, but how ought we to conceptualize the part of the physical world to which that mathematics corresponds? Does the quantum world really entail ‘spooky action at a distance’, as some have thought, so that what happens in one region of space could instantaneously affect some other region in a distant galaxy? (If so, how is that consistent with relativity? How could the scientific project even be possible in such a world?) Is our best theory of the quantum regime ultimately a theory about observers or minds or measurements or consciousness or q-bits of information, and so not really a theory of an independently-existing objective physical world at all? And does chance or indeterminism play a fundamental role at the quantum level, or is it merely a reflection of our own ignorance? If it plays a fundamental role, how do we explain why things happen as they do? As we’ll see, different ways of understanding the laws of quantum mechanics answer all of these questions in strikingly different ways. Not for nothing did Feynman also once say: “I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics”!

This is not a course in the physics of quantum theory, but a course in the philosophy of quantum theory. Although we will (of course) have to learn the basic structure of quantum mechanics along the way, no specific knowledge of physics or philosophy is presupposed and there will be no problem sets. Rather, once we’ve discussed the core principles of the theory, our aim will be to think carefully about the main concepts and investigate ways of conceptualizing how the whole structure fits together. What we’ll discover (as noted above) is that there are strikingly different ways of understanding what the theory is telling us about the physical world, and ingenious and fascinating arguments to the effect that some of those ways are better than others. My aim is not to advocate for a particular answer or picture, but instead to cultivate a sense of the intellectual landscape and debate.

There will be four in-class tests and one final paper. There is an official prerequisite of one introductory philosophy course, which I’m happy to waive if you email me.’

comments.author: Ziya Vhora
comments.text:
hi! I think when traveling to any country and achieving minimum profiency it’s helpful to know things like numbers, how to ask for directions, greetings, and food related vocab.  
you still have plenty of time, so I’d recommend immersing yourself in the language and you can begin by watching Spanish shows in English subs, and esp having someone you can have convos in Spanish with. I think i used to use babbel briefly to learn the language and it was helpful at the time, but Duolingo helps a little too for cosistency. 

The most important thing is costistency and revisiting vocab so don’t set any unrealistic goals or ambitious goals. I’ve been learning Spanish (not self taught) for a long time so I’d recommend you stick to learning the basic vocabulary needed for travelling - though don’t underestimate six months because you might be able  to pick up on the language quickly!

You’ll be able to buy most of the things you need at the convenience store on campus or IKEA, so just bring clothes and products that are exclusively to ur country. author: Nisa Riaz
text:
Full-time Job Opportunity
Software Engineer I | baraka (yc21)

baraka (yc21) is looking for two early-career engineers to join their team.

baraka (yc21) is a fintech platform giving retail investors access to global markets, built on real-time trading infrastructure. You will work closely with our engineering team, gaining direct exposure to how a live trading platform is actually built and operated.

What you'll do:
• Build and maintain services across our order management and event-driven pipelines
• Work directly with Kafka, PostgreSQL and Redis in systems that handle real trading volume
• Collaborate with senior engineers on architecture and design decisions
• Take ownership of features end-to-end, from design through to production

Who we're looking for:
• A degree in Computer Science, Software Engineering, or a related field
• Solid grasp of data structures, algorithms, and object-oriented design
• Strong fundamentals in Java (or equivalent) and a genuine interest in backend/distributed systems
• Familiarity with databases, REST APIs, and version control (Git)
• Self-driven, with a habit of digging into problems rather than handing them off
• Comfortable in a fast-moving, high-ownership environment
• Fintech or OMS exposure is a plus, not a requirement

What we offer:
• Direct mentorship from senior engineers working on production trading systems
• Real ownership from day one, not a rotation, not a sandbox
• Exposure to the full stack of a live fintech platform: Java, Spring Boot, Kafka, PostgreSQL, Redis, AWS, Kubernetes
• Based in Dubai, UAE (hybrid)
• Market-level compensation

Immediate joiners preferred.

If you're excited by hard engineering problems, enjoy learning quickly, and want to work on systems where the stakes are real, we'd love to hear from you.

If you are interested, please send an email with your CV and earliest join date to nisa.shahid@getbaraka.com.

author: Xander Christou
text: Hello! Do you know anyone who has tried out Etihad Rail and would like to share their experience? Interested in hearing perspectives, and also from Fujairah residents considering using it to commute to AD. Thanks in advance!

comments.author: Oscar Wang
comments.text:
Yes, I tried it last weekend. The station in Abu Dhabi is quite far (in Musaffah) from the center but parking is free. The trains are nice and on-time, it will only take you 1h45min to go from FUJ to AUH. Apart from the station location and current frequency of trains, I could not find any down sides as a quite experienced train traveler around the world and enthusiast for public transport.

I would recommend it for commuting if your company is close to the station / any ER shuttle or city bus shuttle stations.

Another concern would be that after opening of new stations later this year, the schedule might be more packed given that it is a mostly single-track, freight-prioritized line. Also, there may be additional stops for AUH-FUJ services, increasing the travel time.

# **[Application Open] - iGEM **

Hey guys!

iGEM is an annual **multidisciplinary Synthetic Biology competition**, where over 400 teams from universities and high schools all around the world work on year-long projects to tackle different challenges and gather at the [Grand Jamboree](https://jamboree.igem.org/2024/home) to present their work.

We currently have a fully formed team, but are looking for a candidate to **join our wiki team**. The wiki team is responsible for designing a website for our project.

**Deadline Aug 8th. **Applications will be reviewed on a **rolling basis** as they are received. Position may be filled before deadline. 

Any questions? Please feel free to reach out to [nyuad.igem@nyu.edu](mailto:nyuad.igem@nyu.edu). You may also chat with any of the 2026 iGEM members (check out our instagram at @nyuad.igem) to hear about their experience.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

**Program Analyst**

Location: Abu Dhabi, UAE | Full-time, office-based
Experience: 1–3 years
Salary: Competitive

**About Brinc**

Brinc is a global venture accelerator and innovation platform that works with ambitious founders, corporates and governments to build and scale the businesses of the future.

We are expanding our UAE team following the launch of a major new partnership with one of the country's largest and most prestigious accelerator platforms. This is our newest client engagement and one of our most exciting programmes to date, offering the opportunity to work at the centre of the UAE's rapidly growing entrepreneurship ecosystem.

**The Role**

We are looking for a highly driven and exceptionally organised Program Analyst to support the successful delivery of our accelerator programmes in Abu Dhabi.

This is a hands-on role for someone who thrives in a fast-moving environment, takes pride in operational excellence and genuinely loves entrepreneurship. You will work closely with founders, mentors, investors, partners and senior stakeholders to ensure every aspect of the programme is delivered to an exceptional standard.

The ideal candidate will have between one and three years of professional experience, strong analytical and organisational skills, and a real hunger to learn, contribute and grow.

**Key Responsibilities**

• Support the day-to-day planning and delivery of accelerator programmes.
• Coordinate programme schedules, workshops, events, meetings and founder activities.
• Maintain accurate trackers, programme documentation, databases and reporting materials.
• Monitor startup progress, milestones, participation and programme KPIs.
• Conduct research on startups, sectors, markets and emerging technology trends.
• Support startup sourcing, application reviews, assessments and selection processes.
• Liaise with founders, mentors, speakers, investors and ecosystem partners.
• Prepare presentations, briefing documents, reports and stakeholder updates.
• Anticipate operational challenges and take ownership of resolving them quickly.
• Support major programme moments, including selection days, bootcamps, investor events and demo days.
• Help ensure every founder and stakeholder interaction reflects Brinc's standards of quality and professionalism.

**What We Are Looking For**

• One to three years of experience in programme delivery, consulting, startups, venture capital, innovation, operations or a related field.
• A genuine passion for entrepreneurship, startups and supporting founders.
• Exceptional organisational skills and strong attention to detail.
• The ability to manage multiple workstreams, deadlines and stakeholders simultaneously.
• A proactive mindset and willingness to take ownership beyond a narrow job description.
• Strong written and verbal communication skills.
• Confidence working with senior stakeholders and external partners.
• Strong research, analytical and problem-solving abilities.
• High standards, sound judgement and a commitment to delivering excellent work.
• Comfort working in a fast-paced, demanding and highly collaborative environment.
• Willingness to work full-time from the office in Abu Dhabi.

**What Success Looks Like**

You are someone the team can depend on completely. Programme information is accurate, deadlines are met, stakeholders are well supported and potential issues are identified before they become problems.

You bring energy, curiosity and urgency to the role. You care deeply about the founder experience, look continuously for ways to improve programme delivery and are excited by the opportunity to help build one of the UAE's most important accelerator initiatives.

**Why Join Brinc**

• Work on Brinc's newest and most exciting UAE programme.
• Gain direct exposure to high-potential founders, investors, mentors and government stakeholders.
• Join a global team working at the forefront of entrepreneurship and innovation.
• Build meaningful experience across venture acceleration, programme operations and ecosystem development.
• Take on significant responsibility early and grow alongside the programme.
• Receive a competitive salary and the opportunity to build a career in one of the world's most ambitious startup ecosystems.
